facts.text: The sun cake is a well-known souvenir pastry of Taichung with a thin, flaky skin and a sweet maltose filling.
One long-established Taichung bakery says the sun cake was first called a malt cake and was renamed after customers suggested a name that was easier to remember.
The wheel cake comes from the Japanese snack imagawayaki and was brought to Taiwan during the period of Japanese rule.
Wheel cakes are cooked in a cast-iron pan with round holes; red bean paste is the classic filling, so they are also called red bean cakes, and custard and other fillings are common today.

Puffed rice cake vendors once traveled the streets by bicycle, tricycle, or cart; rice heated in a pressure pot bursts out with a loud bang when the pot is opened, and is then mixed with syrup, shaped in a mold, and cut.
The ox-tongue cake is named for its long oval shape, which looks like an ox's tongue; the Yilan version is thin and crispy.
The Lukang ox-tongue cake is thicker and softer than the Yilan version and is best eaten warm.

Dragon's beard candy is made by pulling a block of maltose again and again into thin silver-white threads, coating them with roasted rice flour so they do not stick, and wrapping them around peanuts or sesame.
Honeycomb candy is made by heating sugar with a little water in a ladle, taking it off the heat, and adding baking soda; the soda gives off carbon dioxide, so the candy puffs up and is full of holes.
Taiwanese ice pops are made by pouring juice, sugar water, red bean soup, or milk into molds, adding bamboo or wooden sticks, and freezing them.
Many sugar factories in Taiwan sold ice pops and let street sellers buy them in large amounts.
